clips.title: Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud

extraction.summary: An essay arguing that apps should keep the primary copy of user data on the device, work offline, and sync between devices, and evaluating which technologies can deliver that.

claims.statement: Cloud apps stop working when the server is unreachable or the vendor shuts the service down.
When people edit the same data offline on different devices, the edits must be merged later without losing anyone's work.
Keeping the primary copy of data on the device makes reads and writes fast because they do not wait for the network.
The essay presents CRDTs as a promising foundation for local-first apps.

extraction.summary: An overview of conflict-free replicated data types: data structures that can be updated independently on several replicas and always merge to the same result.

claims.statement: CRDTs merge concurrent updates automatically, so every replica converges to the same state without a central server deciding the order.
A CRDT replica can be updated locally without coordinating with other replicas first.

extraction.summary: Documentation for Yjs, a CRDT library that exposes shared types such as maps, arrays and text, with pluggable providers for network sync and local persistence.

claims.statement: Yjs shared types let several users edit the same document concurrently and merge their changes automatically.
The y-indexeddb provider stores a Yjs document in IndexedDB so offline edits survive a page reload.
Yjs is network-agnostic: sync runs through separate providers such as WebSocket or WebRTC.

extraction.summary: Reference for IndexedDB, a transactional, asynchronous key-value database built into browsers for storing large amounts of structured data, including files and blobs.

claims.statement: IndexedDB is asynchronous and is available both in windows and in workers, so storage calls do not block page rendering.
Because IndexedDB is available inside service workers, a service worker can save its state there and restore it after it restarts.
The low-level, event-based IndexedDB API is verbose, so many projects use a wrapper library.
Every IndexedDB read and write happens inside a transaction.

extraction.summary: A guide to choosing among browser storage mechanisms, recommending IndexedDB and the Cache Storage API and explaining quotas and persistence.

claims.statement: localStorage is synchronous, blocks the main thread while it reads or writes, and cannot be used from workers.
IndexedDB and the Cache Storage API are the recommended places for app data and network resources.
navigator.storage.estimate() reports how much of the quota an origin is using.

clips.title: Storage quotas and eviction criteria - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: Explains how much data an origin may store, how the limit is shared across storage APIs, and when browsers delete stored data.

claims.statement: Data in best-effort storage can be evicted by the browser without asking the user when the device runs low on disk space.
The quota is shared by IndexedDB, Cache Storage and OPFS for the same origin.
Eviction removes all of an origin's data at once rather than individual entries.

clips.title: StorageManager: persist() method - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: Reference for navigator.storage.persist(), which asks the browser to mark an origin's storage as persistent.

claims.statement: Calling navigator.storage.persist() asks the browser to exclude the origin's data from automatic eviction.
persist() resolves to a boolean that tells whether the request was granted.

clips.title: Origin private file system - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: Describes the origin private file system, a per-origin file system that is invisible to the user and offers fast synchronous access from workers.

claims.statement: Synchronous access handles, the fastest way to read and write OPFS files, cannot be used on the main thread.
OPFS lets an app read and write files in place without permission prompts, which suits database engines that need random access.
Files in OPFS are private to the origin and are not visible in the user's file system.

clips.title: Using Web Workers - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: A guide to running scripts in background threads with dedicated and shared workers and exchanging data with them through messages.

claims.statement: Running file and database work in a dedicated worker keeps the page responsive and gives access to APIs that are only allowed off the main thread.
Workers cannot touch the DOM, so results must be sent back to the page with postMessage.
Data passed with postMessage is copied with the structured clone algorithm unless it is transferred.

clips.title: Service Worker API - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: Overview of service workers, which sit between a web app and the network to intercept requests, cache resources and enable offline use.

claims.statement: A service worker can answer requests from Cache Storage, so the app shell still loads when the network or the server is down.
The browser stops idle service workers, so any state kept only in a service worker's memory is lost.
Service workers run only on secure origins served over HTTPS or on localhost.

clips.title: A future for SQL on the web

extraction.summary: Introduces absurd-sql, which runs SQLite compiled to WebAssembly and persists it by storing database blocks in IndexedDB, and measures it against using IndexedDB directly.

claims.statement: Doing many small reads and writes as separate IndexedDB transactions makes an app's data layer slow.
Before persistent backends existed, SQLite compiled to Wasm kept the whole database in memory and lost changes on reload unless the app saved it manually.
Treating IndexedDB as a block device for SQLite and batching block writes into few transactions is faster than using IndexedDB directly.

clips.title: SQLite Wasm in the browser backed by the Origin Private File System

extraction.summary: Announces the official SQLite build for WebAssembly and shows how to persist a database in the origin private file system from a worker.

claims.statement: The official SQLite Wasm build can store its database file in OPFS, so data persists across reloads without an IndexedDB layer in between.
The OPFS-backed database has to be opened from a worker because it relies on synchronous file access.
Using the OPFS persistence requires the page to be cross-origin isolated with COOP and COEP headers.

extraction.summary: Compares the ways SQLite Wasm can persist databases in the browser, including the OPFS VFS and the OPFS SyncAccessHandle pool VFS, and their trade-offs.

claims.statement: An OPFS sync access handle locks its file, so only one connection at a time can use the database and other tabs get errors.
The SyncAccessHandle pool VFS works without COOP and COEP headers, at the cost of supporting only one connection.
A database file on OPFS is read page by page, so the dataset does not have to fit into WebAssembly memory at once.

clips.title: Web Locks API - Web APIs | MDN

extraction.summary: Reference for the Web Locks API, which lets scripts in tabs and workers of the same origin acquire a named lock and coordinate work.

claims.statement: A named Web Lock lets tabs elect a single owner for a shared resource while other tabs wait in a queue until it is released.
A lock is released automatically when the tab or worker that holds it goes away.

clips.title: Up to 4GB of memory in WebAssembly

extraction.summary: Explains how V8 raised the maximum WebAssembly memory from 2GB to 4GB, the limit of 32-bit addressing, and what toolchains must do to use it.

claims.statement: With 32-bit addressing a WebAssembly instance cannot use more than 4GB of linear memory, which caps in-memory datasets.
Linear memory can grow while the module runs but never shrinks.
